opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's been faster than I expected, and in some ways faster than most people outside the field realize.

When we started at the end of 2024, a lot of the conversation was still "can we get a humanoid to walk reliably, can we get a decent dexterous hand at a reasonable cost." A year or so later, many of those basic questions feel much more settled. Locomotion has become close to a commodity. You see many teams with robots that can walk, run, recover from pushes, even do flips, and much of that comes from better actuators plus sim-to-real reinforcement learning maturing very quickly. The supply chain, especially in China, has driven costs down dramatically. Joints, motors, reducers, sensors: prices that seemed unreachable two years ago are now normal.

But I'd separate the "body" from the "useful body." The pace of hardware that looks impressive in a demo has been very fast. The pace of hardware that can work eight hours a day, in a messy real environment, without someone standing next to it, is still much slower. Durability, heat dissipation, hand reliability, tactile sensing, battery life: these are the unglamorous problems, and they don't move as fast as the videos suggest.

The hand is the clearest example. Arms and legs are converging, but there's still no consensus on the hand: how many degrees of freedom, tendon-driven or direct-drive, how to integrate touch. That's where I think hardware is still genuinely open.

So my overall view is that hardware is no longer the main bottleneck it used to be. It's good enough, cheap enough, and improving fast enough that the bottleneck has shifted toward data and the intelligence layer: how you get robots to actually do useful, generalizable manipulation. That shift is part of why we started the company when we did. A few years earlier you'd have spent all your energy just fighting the hardware. Now you can start treating it more as a platform and focus on the models.

r001.rationale: The response says there is still no consensus on hand design and calls it an open hardware problem; it does not predict that dexterous hands will become standard soon.

r002.rationale: It mentions hand reliability and tactile sensing as unresolved issues, but does not explain that they enable more complex or finer-grained tasks.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, faster than I expected, and in a direction I didn't fully anticipate.

When we started at the end of 2024, the conventional wisdom was that hardware was the bottleneck. Everyone said the models were moving fast but the bodies couldn't keep up: the hands were too crude, the actuators too expensive, the whole bill of materials made it impossible to think about scale. I believed a version of that myself. I thought we'd spend the first year or two mostly waiting for the supply chain to catch up.

What actually happened is that the supply chain, especially in China, moved much faster than people assumed. Within about twelve months the cost of a decent humanoid platform came down dramatically, dexterous hands went from a research curiosity to something you could buy from multiple vendors, and the joint modules and motors became almost commoditized. The ecosystem that built up around electric vehicles and drones turned out to transfer very directly. So on the pure component level, I'd say hardware stopped being the constraint sooner than I expected.

But I want to be careful here, because "fast" on the component side can be misleading. The thing that didn't improve as quickly is reliability and consistency. A robot that works beautifully in a demo and a robot that can run eight hours a day for months without someone babysitting it are very different products. Tolerances drift, sensors fail, calibration goes off. And that matters a lot for us, because we're a model company at heart. We need hardware we can collect data on at scale, and if every unit behaves slightly differently, the data is noisy and the policy learned on one robot doesn't transfer cleanly to the next.

So my assessment is roughly this: the question has shifted from "can we build the body" to "can we build the body consistently, and can we build the right body." That second part is interesting. Hardware design is starting to be pulled by the model side. We now care less about whether a hand has twenty degrees of freedom and more about whether its sensing gives the model the signal it actually needs. Tactile sensing, for example, matters more to me than another finger joint.

I'd also say the pace has forced a change in how I think about our own role. A year ago I wondered whether we'd need to build hardware ourselves to control the whole stack. Now I think the smarter position is to stay close to several hardware partners, help shape their roadmaps with what the models need, and not try to own the factory. The hardware will keep getting cheaper and better without us. The intelligence layer is where the real scarcity still is.

r001.rationale: The response says dexterous hands are now available from multiple vendors, but does not predict they will become standard robot equipment soon.

r002.rationale: It says tactile sensing gives models useful signals, but does not explain that dexterous hands and tactile sensing enable more complex, fine-grained tasks.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate the pace of hardware iteration from the pace of making that hardware reliable. Since we started at the end of 2024, my impression is that iteration has been very fast. But a new prototype and a machine that can work consistently are two different milestones.

For us, the important question is how much each hardware revision improves what the robot can actually do. Can it repeat a task reliably? Is it easier to maintain? Does it cost less to operate? That’s how I would assess progress, rather than simply counting new models or looking at impressive demonstrations.
